text: My last thoughts: Peter Eckersley lived a life of principle, brought joy to his friends, engaged deeply in trying to make the world better, and pursued eclectic and multidisciplinary intellectual pursuits with creativity. May we all strive to live up to that excellent example.
It's surreal to have to write this thread. His passing is shocking beyond shocking. A part of me is still fully expecting to get lunch with him and catch up when I finish moving back to the bay area.
From the outpouring of stories people are telling as they celebrate his life and impact, it's clear that my experience with him was far from unique. Peter Eckersley was a good man.
He was also principled and thoughtful in his approach to  mitigating AI risks. He was an excellent colleague. The field has lost someone who had much to contribute.

With his wild hair, occasional flair for theatrical outfits, goofy grin, and enduring kindness, he was an extremely endearing character. I greatly enjoyed the too-short time I got to spend with him. He embodied the spirit of camaraderie.

He was warm, compassionate, and sincerely supportive to me in ways that helped me get through it. We would go for walks around the Mission and have long conversations about life, the universe, and everything. He was always insightful.

My small contribution to the canon of Peter Eckersley stories. We spent the summer collaborating last year at OpenAI. It coincided with a period in my life where many things changed abruptly and I was very lost and depressed.

Outside-view expected value shift: how much value does the event create/destroy? How much do you expect the value of the world state to change or not change by the time of the event? Divide the expected value shift by the event value and get a probability.
Intuition: just guess the probability of the event based on whatever feels right. In my experience intuition usually overestimates.
I come up with two estimates, one based on intuition and one based on the expected value shift (taking the outside view), and then reconcile them.

It's all very tricky. Turns out a lot of people in the world genuinely intend for good outcomes and accept different trade-offs on a lot of axes, and use power to achieve outcomes that reflect their trade-off preferences, resulting in a mix of good and bad that's hard to judge.

As an individual, when trying to honestly evaluate other individuals, you have to very carefully disentangle the stories and facts to figure out under what contexts people had what power and whether they used it responsibly, and/or in accordance with their real principles

Narratives around people's goodness or badness, or ability to contribute to discussion, often rely on figuring out what level of power they have, but usually context is stripped out to meet the needs of the narrative

It's difficult to effect system-level change without exerting power in a way that causes harm or discomfort for some, and this is a challenge for well-meaning people who want systems to change, especially when they care about harm reduction
Whenever you exert power you potentially cause an outcome contrary to other people's preferences, usually (but not always) creating some amount of harm and discomfort
You can expend power by moving current through a wire, and the power given off will be proportional to voltage times current (I promise this is the only lame joke tweet in this thread)

Attempting to cultivate, maintain, or use power can create circumstances where others have stupendous power over you - think of many politicians only allow themselves to say what their audience is open to hearing
Your experience of material circumstances - whether because they're too good or very damaging - can make you unaware of power you can exert, or are exerting, in other settings
You can create power orthogonal to your resources, shared beliefs, and skills by charisma and excitement, but you can't sustain it if you can't ground it in reality somehow
You can create power orthogonal to your resources and punch way above your weight by being highly individually productive and making things people want access to
You can create power orthogonal to your resources and punch way above your weight by tapping into shared beliefs

(I suspect this is largely true of many moderately-known professionals who look high-status but lack super-wealth and consequently live a weirdly fragile existence, at the mercy of the audience's whims or a health incident)

You can have sufficient resources and standing/fame that you appear to have power at the system level but have no ability to meaningfully change what other people do or assure anything but your own material survival
You can have next-to-no power at the system level and have massive power in a much smaller setting
This creates a sort of weird frothiness to who has power and who doesn't and when they do or don't have it, which is all contextual
There's a fractal nature to power dynamics: they exist at the system scale, at every resolution within the system, all the way down to individual interactions between people
Power and power dynamics are weird and I'm not sure people understand them well. Some scattered thoughts and reflections, 🧵

My dad always used to tell me that it was pointless to compare yourself to others. He hated (hates) playing competitive games, because the zero-sumness of it apalls him. He would say, "Only compete against yourself. Try to be better than you were before." 7/
That the negative view was because I was downweighting myself and my own value, not because there was some cosmic truth to my relative worth. 6/
And I realized every single time, if the accomplishment I envied had been my own, I would have still persuaded myself that it wasn't much, that it wasn't good enough, etc. 5/

When I noticed myself doing this too often I started wondering - "Wait. If I had done the thing my peer had done, the thing that I feel inferior in comparison to, would I reach the level of internal peace that I seem to imagine it would confer?" 4/

The trophies, the degrees, the published work: you'll look at all of them and think, "it wasn't much, I didn't really do anything of value." No matter how many you have. If you play the comparison game with peers, you'll always think you've done less. 3/

Celebrate the good. This is a surprisingly not-terrible outcome. There's a lot that is not working as well as it could, but still, quite an achievement has happened here!

It's an amazing amount of social coordination to get from rough consensus among that tiny community of scientists to enough trust that 240 million people will try a new kind of vaccine to protect against a new kind of virus they don't have experience with.
Let's say these are vast underestimates and the community of experts in this space has ~50,000 highly-trained people who have rough consensus. My alma mater has a higher total enrollment than that.
A quick Google search yields numbers like "9,136: Number of infectious disease specialists in the United States" (from WebMD), 2611 for number of members in the American Society for Virology.

But how many people are experts in virology? How many people are experts in mRNA vaccine design? How many people are legitimately qualified to have high levels of certainty that this works as-described, that the safety and efficacy studies are sufficiently exhaustive?
And in many sub-disciplines, the answers that people come up with are very reliably testable and correct. And scientists will get it right, fast, when lives are on the line.

For those of us who are in science, maybe it's a little easier: we know that for all the faults in the scientific community, for all the issues with peer review, for all the poorly-designed incentives in academia, science tends to march on to the correct answer.

And make no mistake: it's a *huge* amount of uncertainty. "Trust the science" is a difficult slogan to rely on when you ask hundreds of millions of people to accept an injection designed and understood only by a very tiny group of experts.

I know a lot of folks are bummed about militant anti-vaxxers and the anti-vax grifters, but it's worth celebrating that in the USA more than 72% of people have at least one dose. That's a remarkable amount of social coordination in the face of high uncertainty.

@rajiinio (And yes... I acknowledge that the word "reasonable" is doing an unreasonable amount of work in this thread, mea culpa)
@rajiinio I think commentary on ML papers is closer to the latter than the former. Especially when it's coming from, like, tenure-track professors.

@rajiinio But if you were running an online discussion community for conversations about a popular TV show, you might reasonably expect people to behave a certain way in your community and impose moderation standards.

@rajiinio IMO what counts as a reasonable expectation for comportment depends really strongly on context. If someone is talking about an issue that impacts their quality of life or their livelihood, it seems unreasonable to expect them to be perfectly calm or well-measured.

@rajiinio I definitely don't think a reaction becomes meritless because of the presence of raw emotions, and I don't think raw emotions should be punished. But for discussion of low-stakes research results released via blog or arXiv, being considerate feels like a fair bar.

@rajiinio Intentional decisions about values in culture are hard to implement, but it doesn't mean we shouldn't try. This thread is more or less a bid that we should have a certain community value about how we treat each other while responding to research.

@rajiinio FWIW, OpenAI gets some amount of exposure to this genre of critique, but is far from the only target. I guess it's difficult to disentangle my institution from my position, but the position I'm taking here is a matter of personal opinion and extends beyond defense of colleagues.

@rajiinio But there are some forms of this that interject unnecessary stress and anxiety into people, without significantly advancing the real scientific goals we purport to share (truth-seeking, developing technology in service of improved standards of living, etc).

@rajiinio I don't think public scrutiny and skepticism are bad; I think these are fundamentally good as mechanisms of truth-seeking. I would like for people to be rigorous in how they evaluate research, and I think there should be gatekeeping in the field for something like rigor.

Write critiques on the merits of the work. On its technical correctness, on its social impact, on whether you think the line of research is likely to be fruitful if pursued by other researchers. If the real-world stakes are low, there is no excuse to be unkind. 7/7

Intentionality is incredibly important for general-purpose risk mitigation. If we don't all get dramatically more intentional about how we build and use AI systems, we'll fail to meet the risk mitigation needs we'll have in just a few years. 6/7

Certainly, many folks in the AI ethics space want to see AI practitioners become intentional because they do not want what is almost certainly going to happen otherwise---a default set of social, cultural, and political consequences. But correlation is not equivalence. 5/7

Intentionality is orthogonal to what preferences you are optimizing for. But AI ethics discourse often collapses this distinction, IMHO, to its detriment---seems many AI practitioners think "AI ethics" is code for a specific set of social, cultural, and political beliefs. 4/7

This is distinct from work that you do to attain a performance target on the task of interest. It takes much more effort because it requires you to model a whole lot of messy, complex interactions between people and technology. Takes more effort => often ignored. 3/7

What do I mean by intentional? I mean---you have done some amount of work to model and plan the scope, scale, and nature of short and long-term impacts from what you did, and you have visibly selected a preferred set of outcomes and can make a case you will attain them. 2/7

There's a central idea in AI ethics I usually see treated implicitly: the question of whether developers are obligated to be *intentional* about what they are building. The position of most ethicists seems to be yes. The default position of developers seems to be no. 1/7

@BlakeleyHPayne I think that's a reasonable basis for critique and I appreciate your thoughts. I agree that there are a lot of unfair elements in the status quo, and certainly that there are cultural expectations about what hard work means that can be exclusionary.

@BlakeleyHPayne Oof, he weighed in somewhere? I think I have him muted. For sure, our field is full of a lot of this kind of baggage, and I'm onboard for calling it out where it occurs. I just don't want us to lose nuance in sub-threshold situations like this.

(This is likely the most controversial thread I've written in a while, and I'm not really looking forward to the inevitable uncharitable interpretations. But I feel confident that the people who work with me know that I will never expect or ask for a 90 hour week.)

Let Greg be Greg. Don't force or pressure anyone to be Greg. Reward people for working in ways that create high quality results and are sustainable for them, whether or not that looks like your personal preference.
But we also create a bad culture when we punish people who are otherwise performing well for having working styles that don't line up with our own preferences and expectations.

Different people have different working styles. We create bad cultures when we start overly rewarding people for working in unsustainable ways, or requiring it, or glorifying it, or subtly punishing people for not doing it.
And I've seen folks sometimes totally ignore all of that advice because they were crazy excited by the problem they were working on. They were getting something out of it.

I've been at OpenAI for years, and I've always stressed to colleagues, mentees, and reports the importance of thinking of work as a marathon and not as a sprint---that they should take time they need to breathe, not work on weekends, not overdo it, take a day off if needed.

My experience whenever I've put in more than 40 hours in a week wasn't that I did it because I was told to or because it was normalized or glorified, but because I was working on problems I couldn't stop thinking about because they were important to me.

My experience inside OpenAI's culture is a lot more balanced than @dlowd's tweet suggests. People value hard work but not overwork and overwork/burnout is seen as a sign that a project needs more support. It's far from perfect but no one is asked to be Greg.

Some people feel intensely motivated by what they're working on and would gladly put as many waking hours as they could into it, because that would maximize their life satisfaction. Those people should be free to do it. They shouldn't be punished for it.
Absolutely no one should have to work a 90 hour week and no one should feel obligated to. But I also think it's weird to police how many hours people work if they're doing what they want to do.

Greg's personal take is that working a 90 hour week is helping him make progress. He's not saying literally everyone has to do that to be valuable. He's not asking for exploitative labor practices. He's doing this because he enjoys it and because it's how he gets results.

Ilya said you have to work hard to make progress in AI, obviously true. Making progress on hard problems requires hard work in general---sometimes you can pull a fast one on a hard problem but that's the exception, not the rule. He didn't say you have to work 90 hour weeks.

Some thoughts: it's harmful to say "You have to work 90 hours per week to be successful," because that normalizes the idea that everyone has to do it. But that's not quite what's happening here and this strikes me as a bit disingenuous.

People will live with AI friends and lovers without having to connect with each other. Freedom from having to put up with the flaws and foibles of other real people is a double-edged sword: we'll be less tolerant of others, but farther apart, so less likely to hurt others.

This all makes me wonder if perhaps it's time for conferences to retire "technical novelty" as a standard. "Novelty of understanding" should be sufficient even if we arrive there using well-known tools.

It's worth noting that this paper is arriving several years later than it could have, and the delay is significant. Years of algorithm comparisons are called into question when something like this comes up. Why wasn't this work done sooner? Because the field keeps punishing it.

What does ICLR think of this paper? Three out of four reviewers voted to reject this work for insufficient novelty. An incredibly important empirical result may not be published because reviewers have failed to understand the needs of the field.  https://t.co/cH4RXaOZs7
The D2RL paper makes the need to investigate this even more salient, by showing you can get a *specific* architecture variant to improve performance *across tasks and algorithms.* Again: amazing.

It's been shown before that varying architecture (tweaking away from the well-tuned island) could hurt algorithm performance. (Figure 2: https://t.co/wNGRwTGs5C) This alone should have been enough for us to notice architecture analysis was being undervalued.

Why should we care about this? Because usually deep RL algorithms are evaluated and compared to each other without ablations on network architecture. Results are presented for an architecture tuned for the specific algorithm and tasks used in the experiment.
Amazingly this holds across several algorithms in a wide variety of tasks. The change in task performance from just the architecture is significant.

Example: Consider this paper on dense architectures for RL (D2RL) (https://t.co/ixGrqFEj2w), which came out this year. What it shows is that if you hold an algorithm constant and vary the NN architecture a certain way, performance improves.

Hot take: deep RL research has stagnated because conferences have created bad incentives, rewarding researchers for vacuous claims of novelty, tenuous-at-best theoretical connections, or SOTA, while punishing boring analysis of the empirical tricks that actually make things work.

I want it to be culturally normal to say "I was wrong, and I'm sorry," and to then do something to fix it---at cost to yourself if that's what it takes.

I want to feel like culture incentivizes us to put principle and evidence above ego and the pursuit of power for power's sake. I want it to be culturally normal to scrutinize your own incentives and where they lead.

I don't know if Twitter's the right place for this kind of reflection, but at the same time I wish it was. I wish we would all ask ourselves these questions more honestly, more openly, more transparently.

Thinking about this a lot lately since there are spaces where I perceive myself as having power. I notice myself making some right calls and some wrong calls. I don't want to ever become comfortable with the wrong calls.

And if you can't make it right---if you're not the right person to be the holder of that power---give it to the person or people who should have it. Let evidence guide where power sits instead of ego.

Be uncomfortable with your own exercise of power. Embrace that discomfort. Interrogate yourself on who it benefits, what it's for, what it leads to, whether it's just. Notice and listen when you don't make the right call and work with affected people to make things right.

To sum up: putting gradient descent into the high school calculus curriculum is almost certainly worth it, given how little modification to existing course material it would take, and how much upside it creates. 23/ #education #AIeducation #mathchat #iteachmath @CollegeBoard

This is neatly in-line with recommendations made by educational initiatives like AI4K12 (https://t.co/4tmj5gIA60), which recommends that high school students should be prepared to train simple neural networks. Gradient descent is necessary for that. 22/
Is this material at the right level for high schoolers, and should high schoolers be learning it? Yes and yes! Right level: as mentioned, a direct and small extension of existing material. 21/

From there you can connect it to regression: finding a "line of best fit" by iteratively minimizing mean-squared-error with gradient descent. A student who learns this material now has a conceptual foundation for modern ML techniques. 20/

Intuitively, this is like trying to walk down a hill while blindfolded. All you have to do is check the slope of the ground under your feet (the derivative of the function), and take small steps down the slope (gradient "descent"). 19/

You want to solve a problem min_x f(x). Try an initial guess of x_0, and pick a "learning rate" alpha. "Descend" towards the solution by iterating x_{i+1} = x_i - alpha * df/dx|_(x_i). For small alpha, you get close to a local minimum of f eventually. 18/
The basic lesson fits in three tweets. 17/

How does gradient descent fit into a calculus curriculum? Simply put: it's already halfway there! But underemphasized, incomplete. Key related concepts (like extrema of functions and Euler's method) are presented already, so it's a small change to add this as well. 16/

Putting it all together: ML-based AI technology is going to be central to economic trends over the next decade (https://t.co/4hNjcbdNuM), and gradient descent is a cornerstone concept required for working in ML or understanding ML. 15/
The increased demand for AI is also driving a boom in computer hardware markets (https://t.co/inBHd6HHjV) that's translating directly into AI-centric jobs there as well (https://t.co/9h1B5yQ2H7). 14/
This technology will become increasingly vital to progress in healthcare (https://t.co/PU94fYB0w7), robotics (https://t.co/FxuajDrAS6), and autonomous vehicles (https://t.co/pf2Cc5CeAd).  13/

The basic formula is [data + neural networks + gradient descent = something remarkably useful]. And while this technology is already in use in the applications I mentioned above, there are many more in development: applications are abundant and demand is high. 12/

Neural networks are now being used by companies like Google and Facebook to provide many services to their users, including translation (https://t.co/wlsTzbPfb7), image classification (https://t.co/auANJxSWWz), improvements to search, and more (https://t.co/tLjGr2BndK). 11/

Gradient descent is the algorithm that makes ML-based modules called "neural networks" capable of doing basic intelligence tasks. By an intelligence task, I mean something like looking at a picture and recognizing that there's a bird in it, or picking the best move in a game. 10/

Importantly, gradient descent has become the backbone of an emerging technology field: artificial intelligence (AI) powered by machine learning (ML). The connection is a bit tricky to explain, but I'll give it a shot below: 9/

The cost/benefit ratio for learning it is ridiculous: it's a tiny extension of basic calculus. It wouldn't add more than a couple of pages and a single problem section to any standard textbook. But it unlocks a whole world of problem-solving. 8/
It doesn't always give you a perfect solution, and it is by no means the right tool for every task. But it can get you really, really far, depending on various technical conditions. 7/

"Gradient descent" is an algorithm for finding solutions to optimization problems. It's surprisingly simple, but the simplicity is profound: it is enormously versatile and you can use it to make progress on _any_ mathematical optimization problem. 6/

This is one of the most important concepts in the economy, given how many sectors it touches. So if a student has mastery over formulating and solving optimization problems, they have a foot in the door to a huge range of careers. 5/
If you have a decision-making problem that you can model mathematically, you can write a mathematical optimization problem whose solution is the best possible decision (when the model is good). 4/

Background: Mathematical optimization is core to many economic sectors. Off the top of my head: prominent in operations research and logistics, engineering (for pretty much every engineering field in one form or another), economics, and more. 3/

text: @brungl_ But for some things, which you may or may not be talking about, there's a huge amount of well-documented history that those things do push people towards committing harm.

@brungl_ My principle of charity is coming up on its limits here, since your framing isn't founded in real, comprehensive, systematic risk analysis and truth-seeking, and seems designed at justifying certain things on the basis that they "won't push people towards" harm.

@brungl_ More often than not, when risks are not known to decision-makers, it's because they inadequately assembled  existing information that they could have used. Not because the risks weren't predictable. This is a well-known phenomenon in safety.

@brungl_ My point is that: 1) there are such things as information hazards, 2) decisions about how and when platforms disburse information should depend on a well-calibrated harm calculus, and 3) the level of rigor in that calculus depends on the risks. Higher harm => more rigor.
I hope this helps. Please do your best. I'll do my best too. 24/24

We enable injustice when we measure things as "all good" or "all bad." We create power and exercise power in a million little actions and judgments, and this kind of thing---evaluating complex work all in one direction or another---is one of those ways. 23/24

Normally I like to tie up long opinion threads with a nice bow---I don't have one here. This is a thread about messiness. The world is messy, virtue is messy. You can try hard to be good and still hurt people. We can praise people for trying and also acknowledge the outcomes. 22/

To be clear: I am definitely NOT saying "Scott is a racist" or "Scott is a sexist." If that's your takeaway about my opinion, you are mistaken. My opinion is that we shouldn't paint a complex situation with a broad brush that elides over challenges to our worldview. 21/24

I don't have a firm answer, overall, on the question of "is SSC net good, or net harmful?" when considering the full record. This question is separate from "should SSC exist?" and "did SSC do any good?", and I do think the answer to those two questions is yes. 20/24

I think Scott sincerely tried to set the bar in the right place. But that isn't, in itself, sufficient to make the claim that he succeeded at putting the bar in the right place. I'd venture that sometimes he did and sometimes he didn't. And we shouldn't look away. 19/24

Similarly, on truth-seeking for controversial topics---if you know that certain claims (whether true or not) will give power and support to people who explicitly intend to cause harm, you have an obligation to set the bar on the claims proportionally high to the harm. 18/24

An analogy I'll use here is medical false positives. A patient is tested for a condition whose treatment will be fatal if the patient isn't really sick. The false positive rate for the test is X%. Designing the test so that X is very small is critical. 17/24

I want to be clear that I don't think there is something fundamentally wrong with truth-seeking on charged, controversial topics. But there is a special level of consideration needed for truth-seeking when dimensions of harm are important. 16/24

Yes, he wrote things that were extremely reasonable, he focused on evidence, he tried to be thorough about claims. He explicitly disavowed racism and sexism and tried to make this as clear as possible. He cared about truth. But. BUT. 15/24

Scott Alexander has written some really incredible articles that articulate deep, complex thoughts in accessible ways, helping people become more charitable, compassionate, and open-minded. He also wrote things that gave comfort and power to racists and sexists. 14/24

It's important to me that we can honestly acknowledge that doing good things doesn't make someone or something a universal or perfect good. And especially that what's good for me, or you, is not good for everyone. 13/24

On 2: Is SSC a vital source of "great thought?" I'll be one of the few people to take a somewhat contrary stance to many in my circle: the record is mixed. Most of what he writes is useful and important, and many values he espouses are good and pure of heart. But not all. 12/24
So overall---my calculus is that the NYT is in the wrong. It's important to protect Scott's anonymity. De-anonymizing him is a harmful action not in the public interest. 11/24

If his online work was strongly dependent on information solely available to him through the continued access to being employed in his profession, it would make more sense to connect his online and offline identity for accountability. But that's not the case. 10/24

It really does mostly seem to hurt the people he works with, and his employer. Psychiatric relationships are hard to replace. They're founded on trust build up over a long time. There's no overnight transition that doesn't disrupt his patients' lives substantially. 9/24

If the leverage is exercised, and his personal life suffers (through exposure to physical violence and damage to his professional life), he doesn't lose any of the things that gave him power in his identity as an online author. The use of leverage doesn't accomplish the aim. 8/24

Is that accountability properly obtained by revealing his true name? I honestly don't think so. It grants some people slightly more leverage over him to modulate what he says and how he uses his power. But not much, and it's not clear using that leverage serves anyone. 7/24

In Scott's case, this is tricky because he has two mostly-separate identities, one of which has comparatively minimal power, and one of which influences powerful people and as a result has more power. It makes sense to hold the latter accountable to the public at large. 6/24

That is, the amount of accountability people have should in some sense be proportional to the power they have. Most people seem to agree to this; it's baked into the social contract for democracies. 5/24

The modal answer, I'd guess, is "Almost no one should suffer physical violence from such exposure, and we should grant people privacy to free them from mob justice. But depending on how much power people have and how they use it, we may have a right to know who they are." 4/24

The strongest counterargument to that centers on accountability. In general: should someone be able to use an anonymous platform to influence the public, without having potential consequences to their private, professional life? 3/24

On 1: I think the argument that NYT shouldn't deanonymize Scott Alexander because of the potential harm to his life and patients is a strong argument. Revealing Scott's name is bad for almost everyone involved, there's no benefit to the public for it. 2/24

I have complicated feelings about the SlateStarCodex issue, because it looks like most of the discussion has collapsed the separate questions of 1) is it right for the NYT to reveal Scott Alexander's true name? and 2) is SSC itself a vital source of "great thought"? 1/24

text: It's more than just data. It's how you mathematically create outcomes from the data. Different choices of math / algorithm result in different models and user realities. In honesty, I'm confused that anything in the ballpark of this point is contentious.

No one is trying to argue that logistic regression is intrinsically biased. But it is unequivocally true that when you combine choices of objective functions and data to produce models that behave a certain way, algorithmic choices contribute to outcomes, including bias.

If you're using semantics to fight a strawman about bias in algorithms---"It's just math, the underlying algorithms can't be biased"---you're missing the point / not listening. Algorithm is a broad word, bias comes from many factors, choice of math for a problem setting matters.

I'll err on the side of good faith and note it probably wasn't meant this way, but this is what tone policing and condescension look like. It's so easy to fall into the trap of thinking you are serving a worthy ideal when you are, in practice, being rude and dismissive.

It's easy to imagine we live in a perfectly rational world, where when a technical mitigation exists, adoption is trivial. But history has shown repeatedly that organizations can fail to make the right decisions, even if they are actively trying to mitigate risk.

Safety culture is a critical blocker. If we don't address this with the same level of fervor as we are attacking purely technical mitigations for AI risk, those mitigations---even when fully developed---might simply not get incorporated into deployed systems.

I'll add some clarifications: I definitely don't mean "alignment is unimportant." Alignment is super important. But I think the field has built up a pretty strong body of work on alignment, and comparatively little on safety culture.

Personal opinion: the most important problem in AI safety right now isn't alignment, it's ensuring safety culture is correctly embedded into the human and organizational factors that govern dev/deployment. This requires us to engage with lessons learned from safety outside of AI.

Nabu's pitch: they would use your CDPP data to make you a personal assistant that would also watch ads for you, and you'd get a living wage. It burned me up a little, thinking about how my soul was grist for the machine. But it wasn't much of a choice. (14/25)

When Nabu came along, I was living in a one-bed New York apartment with cracked paint, asbestos, and a cadre of cockroaches that refused to pay rent. I'd given up writing, and I temped at an NYU robotics lab as a mocap actor for grad students building motion datasets. (13/25)

Then in the early 30s, it all started moving towards AI-generated microfiction and short stories targeted at audiences of one. Hard to compete with that. Who needs the great American sci-fi future novel when you're already living in one? (12/25)

I had a few ghostwriting gigs to make ends meet, mostly junky political vanity projects, and it turned out the AI could do those pretty well. Along with anything else that neither had, nor needed, a human soul. (11/25)

In the late 20s, language models started getting good enough that they could generate serviceable boilerplate prose from an outline. Authors didn't go obsolete, but it didn't take much for the bottom to fall out of an already hard profession. (10/25)

I didn't want to depend on that money, but I had to. I was an author in the 20s, and I like to think I was pretty good at it---I published a few books, and even though I didn't notch a best-seller, they meant a lot to the people who read them---but it didn't last. (9/25)

Then came the waves of "link your account to your data." You'd get micropayments by direct deposit every time the account used your data to answer a query from an advertiser. It wasn't much at first, but after Nabu it was enough to get by on. (8/25)

There were holy wars on Reddit about that, but I didn't really understand them. It didn't make a difference to me whether my data was all in one place run by the government or split into thirty horcruxes owned by a bunch of whiny tech billionaires. (7/25)

At some point CDPP hit. "Consolidation of Data and Personal Privacy Act," it was a big deal. A new wave of click-through notifications about how your data would get centrally stored, how you owned your own data, how you could collect fees on its use. (6/25)

I had really mixed feelings about that one. I didn’t know I had to opt out of "send without asking," and it struck up a chat with an old flame from high school about my imminent divorce. It worked out, and we had a good time, but that was goddamn weird. (5/25)

Emails and texts started writing themselves. Facebook set up "Keep in Touch"---all you had to do was write down some stories about your friends, and then if you ever went too long without talking it knew how to get you going again. (4/25)

I vaguely remember the crossover from recommendations to generation. In the mid 20s, Spotify playlists started mixing in new tracks composed by AIs just for you and no one else. Eventually it was all AI tracks, tailored to whatever was going on in your life. (3/25)

It happened so gradually I didn't see it coming. My memory of the internet from the 20s and 30s is a blur of clicking away warnings and notifications about data collection. So what if Amazon, Google, and Walmart were figuring out what kind of--cough--books I liked? (2/25)

The first words I wrote down for this were: "Synthetic touch and smell. The sweet, minty aroma after the electric rain."

It struck me as likely that this kind of pattern should repeat whenever a weird new tech medium comes along, and brain-computer-interfaces would be really exciting for this. Also inspired by @jackclarkSF's Tech Tales in his Import AI newsletter (https://t.co/7UOjVIt3Ke)!

Postscript: Earlier I was listening to some old midis I loved from the early 2000s web, and thought about how tech limitations have led to the emergence of new and beloved aesthetics like pixel art and chiptune.
You can find rainsites these days, but it's just different now. Now, they really feel real, exactly the same as meatspace, and it's great, don't get me wrong, but back then--- (11/11)

The raw roundtrip---brain to plug to plug to brain, none of the modern augmented reconstruction---cut out half the details and kept the strangest parts. I remember the electric rain smelled like mint. (10/11)
My favorite---it was a personal Blinksite, anonymous. A sensory blog from someone who lived somewhere tropical, and every day they'd go sit out in the rain for ten minutes and upload it. (9/11)

Then you could reach out with your hand and turn the world. Touch an ocean, feel the slosh of the waves. Touch a continent, feel the mountain crumbs and sandpaper deserts. Then pick where you want to go, any of the Blinksites, and be there. (8/11)
Like most of the other freaks, I got addicted to that feeling. Nothing like a little bit of infinitely falling into the cosmic abyss to get the day started, I always said. (7/11)

---they couldn't inject for every sense at once, so you'd feel yourself sitting somewhere like you were in real life, gravity pulling on you, but it would make you see this great big sphere below you, and you'd get the fight-or-flight: I'm gonna fall... (6/11)

The startup sense ran a chill and a jolt down your back at the same time. And then it would hijack your eyes and you'd be standing outside of the world. You've got to understand, it wasn't polished and corporatized like it is now--- (5/11)
The plugs weren't great in those days. The bandwidth was terrible, and if you twitched wrong you'd skip a sense. But the content... the content was incredible. (4/11)
And you were terrified, absolutely terrified, of breaking it and giving yourself brain damage. (3/11)

Getting the plug installed felt sketchy, even though it was all legit and above board and the FDA had approved it. When you had one, you hid it, you kept your hoodie up and didn't flash it in public. You were a freak in a secret club. (2/11)

(A sci-fi story.)

The early days of the Blink (Brain-Link) were surreal in ways I can barely remember. In the beginning it was just a bunch of us hackers, because it was too weird for anyone else to want to touch. (1/11)

(fin.)

Policymakers shaken by the COVID19 crisis wake up to tail risks and long-term risks they had previously discounted or ignored, now that they've experienced one explode in their faces. Obvious: govts double down on world health coordination, pandemic prep.

Natsec concerns about supply chains for coping with pandemics/other tail risks lead to shift in priorities on international trade. Not uniform protectionism: new focus on building and safe-guarding home medical supply chains and trying to make other countries depend on yours.

Medicare-for-all doesn't materialize in US, but new regulations on pricing/insurance cos, aggressive red tape cutting on private providers, new advances from publicly-funded health science, and industry appetite to build anew combine to make US healthcare finally sane/afforadble.

Unemployment everywhere shifts up by 5-10 percentage points as new normal, but tolerable due to basic income and expanded social safety nets in most countries. Projected to increase further over time as AI+robotics decrease demand for unskilled and skilled labor.
2024-2030: There is no return to pre-2020 normalcy. But there is a new normal, and it's stable and tolerable to most. Economies grow and recover but in unfamiliar ways.

Mix of worldwide suppression and mitigation measures pay off and hold worldwide death toll below 10M from 2019-2021. A vaccine is developed and established as safe+effective by mid/late 2021, widely deployed early 2022. In many countries, zero new cases in 2023. Pandemic over.

Because of basic income, opportunities in cities no longer uniformly outweigh quality of life cost. Plus, the mass quarantines resulted in many successful WFH/remote work experiments: most businesses now have sufficient experience with this that they can bet longer-term on it.

Deurbanization becomes significant trend for multiple reasons. Fastest-acting reason: hardest-hit cities decline as spooked public moves to less-urban areas for personal health concerns. Longer-term reasons: economic incentives are fundamentally changing in permanent way.

Cold war between China and USA becomes more pronounced. China capitalizes on US weakness, projects appearance of strength with propaganda and occasional adventurous behavior, aggressively messages that US is in decline. Never needs to turn hot to be effective, so it doesn't.

Public funding for medical research soars. National security and public health are now fully recognized as intertwined, and medical manufacturing continues to flourish. Medical and AI begin to dovetail as new AI capabilities allow unbelievably cheap and scalable diagnostics.

Lots of setbacks getting people back to work. Biggest: megaco's accelerate drive to replace virus-susceptible service workers with robotics+AI solutions, drone delivery. Demand for robots and tech specs are finally meeting due to recent advances.

High uncertainty, slow bounceback, and lots of stimulus money for airlines, travel, tourism, and more. Some chaos where companies get nationalized. Uncertainty impacts energy: oil up at stimulus news, stabilizes a bit below pre-pandemic as real demand becomes clear.

2021-2023: New govt leaders around the world preside over a slow, painful recovery by introducing a series of reforms. Basic income is introduced in many places as a temporary measure, though clearly will be impossible to dislodge.

Late 2020: Developed world on war footing with virus. Economies transformed to support the fight. Food, medical, information, and e-tail sectors deliver big. Economic depression for most, esp service sector. No end in sight for fallout => social unrest => political action.

@catherineols @zacharylipton @ilyasut @OpenAI In something like a Tweet, where your space is constricted to a ridiculous degree, you should try to communicate whatever idea is actually most valuable to the audience for the audience. (2/n)
